title: 100-player roguelike
author: meshifthenelse
selftext:
I'm working on a multiplayer roguelike, aiming for 100 people at a time. 

Correct me if I'm wrong, but I don't seem to have seen any such game even from studios and neither posted in subs like this. Which makes me skeptical if I'm missing something?

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: Multiplayer isn’t a good fit for a roguelike. The core of a roguelike is that the player increases skill with each run and goes deeper on the next run. Any multiplayer game is going to have to deal with players at varying skill levels; calibrating difficulty so that the run is going to be fun for everyone is, at best, an unsolved problem.

replies.body: I don't see how making a game where you pick up random items with different functions a bad fit. That's just like any pvp game where you have to find your own guns, but on a higher level.

No you are not 😚
There is a reason there are not a lot massive multiplayer games. You will be spending the next 3 years building a custom engine which you will never finish. Ai is only as good as the user, if you don't have a lot of experience doing that, don't do it. 

I tried and the most I could do with Claude without that experience Was 24 players. 

Im Not trying to be mean, but tell ai: "roast me" and read it!

Instead, try to build and finish a game in a weekend. If you can't, don't bother trying 100 players. 
Just have fun building small, you burn yourself out starting big without knowing the consequences.

comments.author: daddy_reloaded
comments.body:
Do you have some experience in game dev?
If not, start with offline games (several not 1), before.
If you are, then you should probably understand that 100 players need a dedicated big infrastructure to run only one session. If you expect thousands of players, you will need to spend a lot of money on servers infra. That's for the money side. 
For the "dev" technical part, synchronizing 100 players is not that easy, you need a kind of gameplay that allows it. 
And the most difficult part will be the testing part. You will need a lot of testers, serious testers, good luck to find hundreds of testers...

Well I'm a software engineer by trade so I have general experience with distributed systems etc.

You might be better reworking your idea into something that brings together the gameplay of many people, but asynchronously. Examples I can think of are The Bazaar or Backpack Battles, but that is just for 1vs1 battles.

comments.author: AdHom
comments.body: I guess it depends on what you mean. Extraction games like Dark and Darker are sort of multiplayer Roguelites. But overall I'd say the concepts just don't mesh very well, and massively multiplayer games are a huge development lift, operating cost, and require mutual buy-in of a large audience to work at all rather than enabling slow growth. Even conventional MMOs are too financially risky for studios to try very often, nevermind an unconventional genre bend and a solo developer. That's probably why you haven't really seen it

comments.author: Traditional-Wish-728
comments.body:
Don’t let people discourage you. If you build it they will come. Here’s a good read on how RuneScape was able to run on a 56k dial-up connection. I would suggest just understanding and minimizing what data actually needs to be sent to and from the client. If you’re running a single dev operation, I’m just assuming you don’t have a huge budget for tons of AWS compute and keeping 100 websockets connected. So you need to really minimize the data being sent

https://jkm.dev/posts/how-2004-runescape-fit-a-multiplayer-rpg-into-56k-dialup/

replies.author: meshifthenelse
replies.body: Thank you! That is really helpful

comments.author: IDMyourmom
comments.body:
The population problem is bigger than the netcode problem, getting 100 humans into one session. Start with 8 players plus 92 bots and get that fun. Decide what 100 players actually do. A roguelike run is about one person’s build and permadeath. What happens when you die at minute 3, and do your choices matter in a crowd? Realm of the Mad God is the closest precedent I know of.

Separate simulation from presentation immediately. I’m on a 16 v 16 game with headroom for more, and I’m paying now to move the sim out of engine scripts into a compiled core. Moving just movement and collision cut our mean tick from about 14 ms to about 8 ms.   
  
Build a headless bot match before you build content. Fixed tick, N simulated players, a number for milliseconds per tick. You want to know your cost per player in week one, not month six. Make it deterministic and hash the state. Record inputs, hash the world every so often, and replay. It’s the cheapest bug finder there is. Watch for floating-point differences across machines; we had results differ in the last bit between Mac and Windows because of trig functions.

comments.author: WoodpeckerWorldly598
comments.body:
Mutliplayer roguelikes are in the form of autobattlers like Hearthstone Battlegrounds and Teamfight Tactics.  
Same premise as the general design of a roguelie but they're multiplayer.

Draft -> Battle -> Draft -> Battle.

Those are just games I'm familar with too, so safe to assume there's probably other types of games that follow that same format.

Just because the term multiplayer roguelike isn't used, does not mean it doesn't already exist.
